e874f1181e68.headline: Meta removes AI-training scraping clause from commercial terms after publisher backlash
e874f1181e68.dek: Meta deleted language letting it use content from business accounts' linked websites to train AI, a day after Nieman Lab reported it, saying its crawling practices have not changed.
keyPoints: Meta's commercial terms, due October 30, let it crawl domains tied to business accounts and use content to 'train' its products; the clause was removed October 17.
Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says there is 'no change to how Meta uses web crawlers' and that robots.txt preferences still apply.
Cornell's James Grimmelmann told Nieman Lab the terms were permission to train AI on any content from publishers' sites, possibly in competition with them.
Andy Stone, Meta's communications VP, said the aim was pulling product information from third-party sites for ad recommendations, not scraping news sites.
Ars Technica found the 'test credentials' language was new to the commercial terms, which experts said could allow paywall bypass.
e874f1181e68.context: Meta has signed AI licensing deals with outlets including CNN, Fox News, USA Today and People Inc., while news organizations and AI companies fight over whether training without a license is fair use. Meta won a high-profile copyright case last year, but other suits against AI firms, including Meta, continue. Meta recently launched a Meta One subscription that charges businesses to post links.
e874f1181e68.whatsNext: Watch whether publishers and legal experts judge the revised commercial terms, which take effect October 30, to be free of the broader crawling and training permissions.

whatHappened: Meta has removed language from its commercial terms that experts said could let it scrape websites linked to business accounts and use the content to train AI. The Verge reported the change on October 17, a day after Nieman Lab flagged the clause and the terms drew criticism from legal experts and publishers.

The deleted sentence said Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages or URLs to 'provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of' its products and services. The terms, due to take effect October 30, apply to business accounts across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger. They also authorized automated crawlers and 'test credentials' to access linked content, and said businesses that disagreed could stop using Meta's products for commercial purposes.

Meta first called the change a consolidation of its commercial and self-serve ad terms. Spokesperson Daniel Roberts said any suggestion that crawling had changed was false. After the removal, Roberts said the crawling terms 'only applied to our ads and business products,' that Meta has clarified this in the terms themselves, and that the updates do not supersede robots.txt preferences.
whyItMatters: For publishers, the stakes were licensing leverage. Nieman Lab noted that virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account. Matt Topic, an attorney at Loevy & Loevy, said the provision would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market. Three legal experts told Nieman Lab it was unclear whether a court would enforce the terms, but they could be used to argue Meta may scrape news sites.

Ars Technica added that the 'streamlining' claim looked weaker on inspection. It found 'test credentials' absent from Meta's existing commercial terms, product catalog terms and ad creative generative AI terms. Meta pointed it to a seller agreement that uses similar wording but is limited to e-commerce listings. Legal experts also raised the antitrust concept of tying, since Meta had begun charging for links it could crawl for free.

The episode lands as Meta faces separate copyright litigation over AI training data. Ars Technica reports a magistrate judge has ordered Meta to identify executives who authorized downloading books from shadow libraries. That case is distinct, but it shows how closely courts are examining how Meta sources training data.
whatToWatch: The revised terms are due to take effect October 30. Publishers and lawyers will likely check whether the final text leaves any broader crawling or training rights, and whether the 'test credentials' language remains.
Meta says robots.txt remains the way for content owners to signal preferences. Whether courts treat such signals as binding is still open, and pending fair use cases could shape that.

f16aefe89a6e.headline: OpenAI claims proofs refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis and resolving Kakeya
f16aefe89a6e.dek: OpenAI announced results in math, computer science and physics, including a claimed refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, but researchers and its own math advisers criticized handpicking experts to review them first.
keyPoints: OpenAI says its model proved local smoothing in all dimensions, which would also resolve the Kakeya and Stein restriction conjectures; the math output was released directly.
OpenAI says its model refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis; Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams will lead review, and the write-up and Lean proof are on GitHub.
The physics result, a claimed existence proof of QCD-type quantum field theories, is unreleased; a group led by David Gross will shepherd it.
OpenAI's math advisory panel AGMAI said a day earlier that AI firms should not give select people early access, and urged public release of the physics outputs.
Anthropic says it released its own refutation of the ETH hours after a Anthropic mathematician suggested OpenAI's work built on earlier results.
f16aefe89a6e.context: The Exponential Time Hypothesis, proposed in 1999, underpins much of computational complexity theory. OpenAI's announcement comes less than a month after it released hundreds of math manuscripts at once, which mathematicians said overwhelmed them. The dispute over how AI labs should release results has become a running argument with the field.
f16aefe89a6e.whatsNext: Watch whether OpenAI publishes the physics proof and Lean output as AGMAI demands, and whether the ETH working group and a proposed conference confirm the result.

whatHappened: OpenAI announced three results in mathematics, computer science and physics, and said it is changing how it releases them after consulting outside experts it calls shepherds. The math result is a proof of Sogge's local smoothing for waves in every spatial dimension at least two. OpenAI says this also yields the Kakeya maximal and dimension conjectures and Stein's spherical restriction estimates across the interior of the conjectured range. The model output was released directly.

The computer science result claims the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false. According to OpenAI, the paper gives a deterministic algorithm that exactly counts satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas in subexponential time and polynomial space; the 3-SAT case refutes the hypothesis. A working group led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams will examine and explain the proof, and at its request the write-up and Lean proof went public on GitHub.

The physics result is described as a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories with gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics. It has not been released. OpenAI says David Gross will lead a group including Michael Douglas, Arthur Jaffe, Igor Klebanov and Nikita Nekrasov to shepherd it. The ETH group also published an open letter asking the community about norms for AI-generated results.
whyItMatters: The ETH has been widely believed and is cited in many papers. Williams told TechCrunch that if the claim holds, much work built on it must be revisited, and that it calls into question intuitions about how tractable hard NP problems are. He said he asked OpenAI whether cryptographic systems were affected and was told they were reasonably confident there were no breaks. TechCrunch reports Anthropic released its own refutation of the ETH hours after Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested OpenAI relied on pre-existing work.

The release process is itself contested. OpenAI's advisory group, AGMAI, said a day before the announcement that AI companies should not designate people to see output first, citing unequal access, borrowed reputation and biased selection. It recommended release on scholarly repositories with Lean-formalized proofs and funding for those doing the checking. Researchers told The Verge that experts welcomed the smaller batch of three results but objected to restricted early access. Andreas Karch called the handpicked group a disaster.

Independent verification is still limited. The Verge notes that varying disclosure and the complexity of the work make it hard for researchers to judge the findings fully, though several experts called them significant or major breakthroughs.
whatToWatch: AGMAI argued that OpenAI says its Lean formalization of the physics work is complete, so there is no scientific reason for further delay, and asked for public release. Whether OpenAI complies, or defers to the Gross group, is the next test.
On the ETH, the working group's review and a conference OpenAI is asked to fund will indicate whether the algorithm stands and what it means for related results.

f1c8e20f7598.headline: YouTube Music adds 'Made with AI' labels to songs as Deezer readies an AI filter
f1c8e20f7598.dek: YouTube Music began rolling out labels on Oct. 14 for tracks made or altered with generative AI, while Deezer said it will add a toggle to hide AI music by year's end.
keyPoints: YouTube Music is rolling out a 'Made with AI' label on the player page for tracks 'altered or fully generated' with AI; the main YouTube app follows later.
Partners can disclose AI use as Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI or No Gen AI. Without disclosure, YouTube says it may use 'other signals', including its own detection tools.
The label does not make a track ineligible for monetization, according to TechCrunch. There is no option to block labeled tracks, Ars Technica notes.
Deezer says it will launch a toggle by the end of the year that removes AI-generated tracks, albums and related artists from search results.
Deezer reported in July that over 50% of daily uploads were AI-generated, around 90,000 tracks per day; a survey found about 45% of its users wanted a way to remove AI music.
f1c8e20f7598.context: Streaming services are splitting between disclosure and restriction as AI-generated uploads grow. Bandcamp has banned AI music, Tidal withholds monetization from it, and Spotify tags AI tracks and says it won't recommend 'AI personas'. Apple Music is reportedly preparing its own AI tags.
f1c8e20f7598.whatsNext: Watch for the label's arrival in the main YouTube app, Deezer's filter launching before the end of the year, and Apple Music's reported AI labels.

whatHappened: YouTube began rolling out a 'Made with AI' label in YouTube Music on Oct. 14. It applies to tracks that were 'altered or fully generated' using AI, including cases such as using a generative model to create the composition and vocals. The label appears on the player page, and tapping it opens a menu with more detail about AI's role. Labels will extend to the main YouTube app later.

Partners uploading music can declare AI use under three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI or No Gen AI, according to TechCrunch's reading of YouTube's help page. Tracks that only use pitch correction such as Auto-Tune fall under No Gen AI. Disclosure is optional. If a partner does not disclose, YouTube says it may use 'other signals', and it says it is working with music partners and using its own detection tools.

Ars Technica reports that Google could also rely on SynthID watermarks for tracks made with Google's AI, and on C2PA metadata used by many other AI music tools. Separately, Deezer said it is building a toggle that hides AI-generated tracks, albums and related artists in search results, due before the end of the year.
whyItMatters: The two announcements show the range of responses to AI music. YouTube is choosing disclosure over restriction: TechCrunch notes AI involvement alone does not make a track ineligible for monetization, and YouTube itself offers AI music tools such as Dream Track. Deezer is letting users opt out entirely. Its CEO, Alexis Lanternier, cited user demand, and Deezer pointed to a survey in which about 45% of customers wanted AI music removed.

Ars Technica raises limits on labeling. Many AI tools leave no identifying mark, so a missing label does not prove a track is human-made. And since listeners often are not looking at a screen, a label is easy to miss. There is also no way to block labeled tracks from playlists, which is the gap Deezer's toggle targets.
The scale explains the urgency. Deezer said AI tracks were 10% of daily uploads when it added detection tools last year and more than 50% by July, which puts pressure on larger services to act.
whatToWatch: Key questions are how accurate YouTube's detection proves when creators do not disclose, and whether the company adds user controls beyond labels. Deezer's toggle is expected before year-end, and Variety reported that Apple Music plans to label AI tracks in the same period.

pullQuote.text: We’ve seen clear user demand for the ability to filter out AI-generated music

f4e0b5373313.context: Apple has been layering Apple Intelligence features into its software, and this extends AI assistants into its productivity and creative apps, where Microsoft and Google already offer chatbots in their office suites. Support for Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting AI agents to apps, signals that Apple is opening these apps to outside agents as well.
f4e0b5373313.whatsNext: Creator Studio updates are due for existing subscribers in November, while the AI assistant continues its beta rollout.

whatHappened: Apple is bringing an AI assistant to its Pages, Keynote and Numbers productivity apps. According to The Verge, the assistant is built on AI models from Apple and OpenAI and can understand a document's context to carry out tasks such as designing, animating and refining slides in Keynote.
Apple says the assistant can draft, restructure and tweak written content in Pages. In Numbers, it can calculate, visualize and organize data, suggest chart types and build custom tables.

The assistant is rolling out in beta to devices compatible with Apple Intelligence, running iOS 27, iPadOS 27 or macOS 27 or later. On macOS 27 or later, the three apps also support the Model Context Protocol, which allows third-party AI agents to plug into them.

Other creative apps are getting updates. Pixelmator Pro adds a Generate Fill feature for editing part of an image by describing the change. Logic Pro for Mac and iPad gets a Liquid Glass redesign, an AI assistant for editing projects, and a redesigned Browser on Mac that uses on-device AI to analyze, classify and tag sounds. Final Cut Pro gains MotionVFX templates, graphics, titles and transitions, plus a Content Hub with stock video, photos and backgrounds.
whyItMatters: The release puts a general-purpose assistant inside apps that many Apple users already own, and it relies partly on OpenAI models alongside Apple's own. The coverage does not say which tasks run on which models or what runs on-device.

Model Context Protocol support may matter as much as the built-in assistant. It means agents from other companies can work with Pages, Keynote and Numbers on macOS, rather than Apple's assistant being the only way to automate them. How widely that is used is not yet clear.
whatToWatch: The Creator Studio updates reach existing subscribers for free in November. The assistant is labeled a beta, so its quality and any changes to availability beyond Apple Intelligence-compatible devices are open questions.
